```{r setup-involvement, include=FALSE}
library(here)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE,
                      fig.width = 7, dpi = 110)
library(remode)          # Hoffstadt et al. (2026)
```

```{=html}
<h1 id="involvement-bimodality">Involvement &times; bimodality (exploratory)</h1>
<div class="block-box">
Does involvement change the <em>shape</em> of the belief distributions? The
theoretical prediction is that more involved respondents hold less nuanced,
more polarised views &mdash; so <strong>bimodality should increase</strong>
with involvement (two peaks at the ends rather than a single central hump).
<br><br>
Each belief item below is split into <strong>5 involvement subgroups</strong>
(0&ndash;20, 20&ndash;40, &hellip;, 80&ndash;100). Pick how involvement is
defined &mdash; each of the five involvement questions on its own, or the five
combined (their mean) &mdash; then <strong>drag the slider from low to high
involvement</strong> and watch each distribution morph. Bars are the
<strong>percentage of that subgroup</strong> (so unequal group sizes stay
comparable); the per-item y-axis is fixed across subgroups so the shape change
is what you see. Small subgroups (low n, shown per item) are noisy &mdash; read
them with care.
<br><br>
Each chart's subtitle reports the <strong>number of modes</strong> estimated by
the <strong>ReMoDe package</strong> (Hoffstadt et&nbsp;al., 2026): a category
counts as a mode when its frequency is <em>significantly</em> higher (bootstrap
test) than the lowest frequency to its left and to its right, applied
recursively.
<br><br>
<strong>How the items are ranked.</strong> There is no standard
&ldquo;modality-increase index&rdquo; in the literature, so the ranking follows
the approach of <strong>Hoffstadt et&nbsp;al. (2025)</strong> &mdash; the same
group as the ReMoDe authors, studying this exact question (involvement as a
polarising factor). Each subgroup's distribution is first <em>classified</em>
from its modality <em>and</em> from whether a mode sits at the neutral middle
category:
<ul style="margin:6px 0">
<li><strong>not polarised</strong> &ndash; unimodal;</li>
<li><strong>weakly polarised</strong> &ndash; multimodal, but a mode still sits
    at the middle category (a moderate common ground survives);</li>
<li><strong>strongly polarised</strong> &ndash; multimodal with no mode at the
    middle (the sample splits into opposing camps).</li>
</ul>
Items are then ordered by the <strong>change in this class</strong> from the
lowest to the highest involvement subgroup. Ties are broken by how many of the
paper's six supporting indicators hold (multimodal at high involvement, unimodal
at low, higher SD at high, smaller share choosing the middle category, larger
median absolute deviation from the scale midpoint, and no mode at the middle).
Both are shown under every chart.
<br><br>
<strong>Steps 1&ndash;6 run the authors' own code</strong>, sourced from a local
clone of their replication repository
(<code>github.com/mfhstdt/involvement_polarization</code>):
<code>split_involvement()</code> forms the subgroups,
<code>mid_prop()</code> the share choosing the middle category and
<code>median_AD()</code> the median absolute deviation from the midpoint.
Their <code>split_involvement()</code> produces <strong>4 quartiles</strong>
(equal-sized groups), which also removes the power problem &mdash; ReMoDe only
declares a mode when a peak is <em>significantly</em> higher than its
neighbours, so a small subgroup returns few modes for lack of power rather than
because it is flat.
<br><br>
The one place we depart from their code is modality itself: they used their
ANAM density method, while we use the <strong>ReMoDe package</strong> &mdash; the
successor method by the same group. ReMoDe additionally returns the
<em>location</em> of each mode, so their &ldquo;is there a mode at the middle
category?&rdquo; criterion (which they judged by eye from density plots) is
evaluated automatically here. Detected modes are <strong>coloured in every
chart</strong>, so the modality estimate can be read directly off the bars.
Set <code>IV_BIN_METHOD</code> to <code>"quantile"</code> (5 quintiles) or
<code>"equal_width"</code> (fixed 0&ndash;20 / 20&ndash;40 bins) to change the
grouping.
<br><br>
<strong>How reliable is each classification?</strong> With roughly 29
respondents per subgroup, a mode count can rest on a handful of people, so every
classification that feeds the ranking is checked with
<code>remode::remode_stability()</code>. That function <em>jackknifes</em> the
distribution: it deletes a growing share of the data (10%, 20%, &hellip;),
re-runs <code>remode()</code> 100 times at each step, and records the largest
share that can be removed while the majority of resamples still recover the
original number of modes. That figure is reported per subgroup as
&ldquo;<em>stable to X% removal</em>&rdquo;, and a comparison is marked
<span style="color:#B22222">&#9888; unstable</span> when either end fails to
survive <code>IV_STABLE_MIN</code> (currently 40%).
<ul style="margin:6px 0">
<li><strong>Only the two subgroups that drive the ranking are tested</strong>
    (lowest and highest), because the check is expensive; results are cached in
    <code>analysis/reports/descriptive_plots/cache/remode_stability_cache.rds</code>, keyed on the count vector, so
    re-knitting is instant. Delete that file to recompute &mdash; it also
    rebuilds automatically once new data changes the counts.</li>
<li>The displayed mode counts always use the <strong>bootstrap</strong> test,
    which the ReMoDe paper recommends at small N. Inside the jackknife the
    faster <strong>binomial</strong> test is used
    (<code>IV_STAB_TEST</code>): it makes the whole grid take about a minute
    instead of ~23 minutes, and on this data it is the <em>more conservative</em>
    of the two, i.e. it errs towards flagging. Set it to
    <code>"bootstrap"</code> for the slower, more exact route.</li>
<li>Flagged items are <strong>still ranked</strong> &mdash; nothing is hidden,
    the marker simply tells you how much weight the comparison can bear.</li>
</ul>
<em>Note:</em> the package's <code>location_stability</code> output is not used,
as it currently returns empty (<code>remode_stability()</code> reads
<code>remode_result$modes</code> while <code>remode()</code> returns
<code>mode_indeces</code>); only <code>stable_until</code> is taken.
</div>

<div class="iv-controls">
  <div><strong>Involvement defined by:</strong>
    <span id="iv-def-buttons"></span>
  </div>
  <div class="iv-sub-row">
    <button class="iv-navbtn" onclick="ivStep(-1)">&#9664; less</button>
    <input type="range" id="iv-slider" min="1" max="5" step="1" value="1"
           oninput="ivSetSub(parseInt(this.value))">
    <button class="iv-navbtn" onclick="ivStep(1)">more &#9654;</button>
    <span class="iv-readout" id="iv-readout"></span>
  </div>
  <div style="margin-top:10px;">
    <strong>Order items:</strong>
    <button class="sort-btn" id="iv-order-btn" data-current="survey"
            onclick="ivToggleOrder(this)">
      Survey order — click to sort by increase in polarisation</button>
  </div>
  <div class="iv-legend" id="iv-legend"></div>
</div>

<div id="iv-mount">
  <p style="color:#999">Loading charts… if this stays blank, open the HTML file
  directly in a web browser (Chrome / Firefox / Edge) rather than the RStudio
  Viewer.</p>
</div>
```

```{r involvement-data, echo=TRUE, results='asis'}
# The analysis is in R/involvement.R; this chunk hands its result to the
# browser, together with the script that draws the charts.
#
# builds iv_data: per belief and policy rule, modality by involvement subgroup
source(here("analysis", "reports", "descriptive_plots", "R", "involvement.R"))

cat('<script>window.IV_DATA = ',
    jsonlite::toJSON(iv_data, auto_unbox = TRUE, digits = 3, na = "null"),
    ';</script>', sep = '')
cat('<script>',
    paste(readLines(here("analysis", "reports", "descriptive_plots", "js", "involvement_browser.js"), warn = FALSE),
          collapse = "\n"),
    '</script>', sep = '\n')
```
